```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4)
library(spLeakage)
```

## Specify the prediction task

A validation split can place test observations close to training data while the
locations where predictions will be used are farther away. The reverse is also
possible. Whether either difference matters for predictive error depends on the
learner, the response process, covariates and the loss being assessed.

`spLeakage` describes this validation–target mismatch. Existing methods including
NNDM and kNNDM also use prediction-target distances and support inspection of their
distributions. The diagnostic is an aid to interpreting a supplied split, not a
certificate that a validation scheme is unbiased.

This example simulates noisy observations of a Gaussian process at clustered
locations. Its covariance is known because we specify it ourselves.

```{r data}
set.seed(3)
n <- 160
centres <- matrix(runif(12, 0.1, 0.9), 6, 2)
xy <- centres[sample.int(6, n, replace = TRUE), ] +
  matrix(rnorm(2 * n, sd = 0.04), n, 2)
xy <- xy %% 2
xy[xy > 1] <- 2 - xy[xy > 1]
d <- data.frame(x = xy[, 1], y = xy[, 2])
D <- as.matrix(dist(xy))
Sigma <- 0.7 * exp(-D / 0.15) + diag(0.3, n)
d$z <- as.numeric(t(chol(Sigma)) %*% rnorm(n))
dep <- list(rho = function(h) 0.7 * exp(-h / 0.15),
            range = 0.15, practical_range = 0.45, signal_prop = 0.7)
```

Our finite prediction target is an equally weighted grid over the unit square.
These locations define the task; they are not additional response observations.
For a real survey, document coordinate units, CRS and any unequal target weights.

```{r target}
g <- seq(0.025, 0.975, length.out = 15)
target <- prediction_target(grid = as.matrix(expand.grid(x = g, y = g)))
folds <- sample(rep_len(1:5, n))
audit <- detect_leakage(d, folds, target, response = "z", dependence = dep,
                        coords = c("x", "y"))
audit
```

## Interpret the quantities

`SLI_rho` is the mean specified correlation for validation nearest neighbours
minus that for target nearest neighbours. A positive value means the former is
larger; a negative value means it is smaller. A near-zero value means the averages
are close, which does not establish equality of distributions or unbiased error.

`SLI_rho2` compares squared correlations. Multiplying it by the marginal response
variance gives the target-minus-validation expected squared-error gap for the
known-mean predictor using one nearest observation under the specified covariance
model. This is not a general identity for full kriging, a random forest or an
arbitrary fitted model.

`A` is the mean target distance minus the mean validation distance. `W` is the
unsigned Wasserstein distance between the two distance distributions. The
inequality `abs(A) <= W` allows opposite differences at different distance scales
to cancel in the signed area. The `crosses` field identifies such crossings
without relying on a small signed score.

```{r ecdf, fig.alt="Validation and target nearest-neighbour distance distributions"}
plot(audit)
```

The local map shows each validation observation's correlation relative to the
average target correlation. It is not a map of target prediction bias.

```{r contributions, fig.alt="Contributions to the signed correlation contrast"}
summary(audit)
plot(audit, which = "map")
```

For observed data, omit `dependence` to estimate an exponential variogram from the
specified response, or supply a scientifically justified model. A nugget is
interpreted as independent observation noise: distinct co-located measurements
have correlation equal to the signal fraction, not one. Marginal response and
model-residual dependence answer different questions. Estimated residuals do not
automatically remove bias from validation.

When a parameter covariance matrix is available, `n_boot` requests approximate
parameter propagation under the fitted family and fixed geometry. Missing
parameter covariance returns no interval. These intervals do not cover predictive
bias, model misspecification or arbitrary uncertainty in the sampling design.

## Compare candidate assessments

A prediction target and a sampling-design label alone do not establish the best
CV scheme. Probability sampling can be clustered, and CV uses smaller training
sets than the deployed model. Recommendations therefore identify assessments to
compare and explain their assumptions.

```{r recommend}
recommend_validation(estimand = "prediction", design = "clustered", target = "grid")
recommend_validation(estimand = "population", design = "probability", target = "grid")
```

The second call concerns assessment of a fixed map using a separate probability
validation sample and a suitable survey estimator. It does not assert that random
K-fold CV is design-unbiased.

```{r rank}
rank_cv_schemes(d, target, response = "z", coords = c("x", "y"))
```

Ranking defaults to unsigned distance mismatch. Selecting a small mismatch is a
comparison rule, not a guarantee that the selected CV error equals deployment
error. Inspect the full distributions and the prediction model before using the
ranking to guide an analysis.

The additional tutorials discuss score comparisons (`vignette("quantify-correct")`)
and descriptive checks beyond spatial distance (`vignette("channels")`).
